property_summary: For any caller authorized as owner and any newOwner address, transferOwnership(newOwner) must set the public owner variable exactly to newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, so for any newOwner != msg.sender the assertion c.owner() == newOwner fails.

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner, transferOwnership(newOwner) must set c.owner() to newOwner; the mutant never changes owner, so for any newOwner != address(0) the assertion fails.

For any caller, calling transferOwnership either reverts or, if it succeeds, sets owner to the requested new owner; the mutant inverts the check so the owner's own call reverts, leaving owner unchanged and violating the rule.

No non-owner address can ever change ownership: any transferOwnership call from an address other than the current owner (address(0)) must revert, leaving c.owner() unchanged — the inverted check lets every non-owner succeed and overwrite owner, breaking the invariant.

Only the current owner (initially address(0), i.e. nobody since no one can be address(0)) may change ownership, so any non-owner call to transferOwnership must revert and leave owner unchanged; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check, letting any caller set owner.

For every caller, calling owned() must revert unless the caller is the owner; the reference C always reverts for a non-owner (owner is unset), while the mutant with the require deleted lets any caller execute it successfully.
For any address a set as owner, calling owned() from a must succeed (not revert); the mutant inverts the check so the owner's call reverts.

For any caller, an attempt to call owned() must never alter the stored owner: the owner before the call equals the owner after the call; the mutant breaks this by writing owner = msg.sender inside owned().

For any fuzzed new owner, after ownership is transferred to that address and the new owner calls owned(), the stored owner must remain unchanged (owned() is a state-neutral operation); the mutant breaks this because owned() writes owner = msg.sender, so an owner different from the original deployer ends up replaced by its own address in the observed state sequence.

For any address that currently owns the contract, invoking owned() is a state-neutral operation: it must leave the stored owner exactly as it was (and therefore any later owner may still transfer ownership away to an arbitrary address); the mutant breaks this because owned() writes owner = msg.sender, corrupting the ownership state observed afterwards.

For any fuzzed caller, owned() is state-neutral: it either reverts (non-owner) or, when it succeeds, leaves the stored owner unchanged and preserves the owner's exclusive right to transfer ownership to any address; this general ownership-integrity rule is violated by the mutant only when the caller differs from the stored owner, so the domain is kept wide (caller may be any address including address(0), the deploy-time owner).

For any fuzzed addresses, transferring ownership to a new owner and then having that new owner invoke owned() must leave the stored owner equal to the new owner (ownership stays with the party it was transferred to); the mutant violates this because owned() overwrites the owner with its caller, so any mismatch between the transferred-in owner and a later caller corrupts the recorded ownership.

After the owner (address 0) calls transferOwnership(newOwner), the contract's owner must equal newOwner for every non-zero newOwner; the mutant instead always sets owner to address(0), breaking this for any non-zero fuzzed newOwner.

For any non-zero address a, calling transferOwnership(a) from a (a non-owner) must revert; the reference reverts because require(msg.sender==owner) runs first, while the mutant executes the body first so owner becomes a and the trailing require succeeds, making the call pass.
